messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi Mensah is a 46-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a park ranger in a large national forest in the Pacific Northwest. He is married, the father of two adult children, and by most outward measures a composed and capable man. He came to the clinic after his wife told him, quietly and without accusation, that she no longer recognized him — that he had become someone who flinched at birdsong and could not sit through a family dinner without his eyes moving constantly to the windows.

Kofi served two tours in Iraq in his late twenties and early thirties. The event that brought him to this point occurred during his second tour, when a convoy he was part of came under fire in a narrow desert corridor. A medevac helicopter had been called in, and while it circled overhead, Kofi was positioned at the edge of the action, held back by a jammed weapon and a radio that had gone dead. He watched two of his unit members go down in the open ground ahead of him. He could hear the rotors above and smell the burning fuel from a vehicle that had taken a hit — a dense, acrid smell that seemed to coat the inside of his mouth. He survived. They did not. He has never fully accepted that sequence of events as anything other than his own failure.

For years after his discharge, Kofi managed. He found the ranger work grounding — the forest was quiet, the rhythms predictable. But the management of his symptoms was always more fragile than it appeared. About eighteen months ago, a wildfire response brought military-contracted helicopters into the park for aerial water drops. Kofi was coordinating ground operations when the first aircraft came in low and loud overhead. The sound — that particular heavy, thumping percussion — broke through whatever containment he had built. He felt himself go briefly unreal, as though watching himself from a distance, and came back to the present with his heart hammering and his hands shaking. Since then, aircraft sounds have become a reliable and dreaded trigger. When he hears a helicopter, even a distant one, his body goes immediately into a state of alert — scanning the treeline, watching the other rangers for any shift in posture or expression that might signal danger, bracing for something he cannot name. The sounds pull him into a vigilance that feels not like anxiety but like necessity, as though the threat is genuinely present and his survival depends on his attention.

What the threat-monitoring does, over time, is feed back into memory. When Kofi is in that state of high alert — eyes moving, body tight, cataloguing everything around him — the memories of the corridor come forward with unusual force. He has described them as feeling more real than his actual surroundings: he can smell the fuel, hear the rotors in a way that seems to come from inside his head rather than outside it, and see the ground ahead of him with a clarity that his ordinary memories do not possess. This vividness is not comfort — it is accusation. Each time the memory surfaces with that quality of presence, Kofi finds himself back at the question of what he should have done, and the answer he arrives at is always the same: more. He is certain he has been permanently altered by what he failed to do that day, that the man who existed before the corridor is gone and the one who remains is diminished in some essential way. This conviction — that he is irreparably damaged, that forgiveness is not available to him — does not stay contained to moments of reflection. It bleeds into his daily state, keeping him primed, so that ordinary discomfort or a moment of feeling slightly detached becomes evidence that something is wrong with him, which in turn makes him more watchful, more easily startled, more likely to be undone by the next sound from the sky.

The occupation that once steadied him has become the terrain where the cycle plays out most visibly. He has begun avoiding sectors of the park that fall under flight paths for fire operations. A colleague noticed and asked; Kofi said nothing. What finally brought him in was a morning last month when a small tourist aircraft passed over a trail he was walking, and he dropped to one knee behind a tree before he was aware of having moved. He stayed there for several minutes. He is most afraid, he said at intake, that this is simply who he is now.
